What is Accounting?
Accounting is an information process, i.e. a method of processing financial information
for different users. Accounting is often been called ‘the language of business’ as it is the
means of communicating financial information. It provides a way of recording, measuring
and describing economic activities.


The accounting function involves identifying, gathering, classifying, recording,
summarising, analysing, reporting and communicating financial information. Accounting
is practical tool used by many in varying jobs. People running a business need an
understanding of accounting to help them make sound decisions about their business.
The Role of an Accountant
As the commercial world has grown in size and complexity, the importance of the
accountant has also increased. The accountant's role has changed as the number of
interested parties has grown. The accountant must prepare information designed to
meet a wide variety of needs and expectations and is responsible to the users of that
information. The accountant's role is dynamic, important and varied. The principal role of
an accountant is to report on the performance of a business. This can involve tasks such
as:
•
Designing, implementing and managing systems for accurately recording and
classifying transactions and other data.
•
Using information obtained to prepare accounting reports which show the
financial performance and position of a business.
•
Communicating the information to all interested parties in a form which the users
can understand.

Areas of Accounting
Financial accountants prepare year-end financial statements as well as analyse and
interpret financial information. Managerial accountants produce, analyse and coordinate
the flow of information which will help in running the business e.g. budgeting, pricing
and planning for future needs. Cost accountants control the costs of producing goods
and services.

Accounting – Unit 0: Introduction and Accounting Cycle
Accounting | Page 1




Auditors check the financial statements to ensure that the financial statements show a
'true and fair view' about the financial affairs of the business. They ensure that the
financial reports comply with regulations. Large companies employ independent auditors
to conduct audits in order to protect the interests of shareholders. Accountants may also
specialise in taxation, investment, estate control, banking or teaching.

Book-keeping Vs Accounting

Bookkeeping is the foundational process of recording financial transactions. It involves:
•
Data entry: Recording sales, purchases, and payments accurately and consistently.
•
Categorization: Sorting transactions into appropriate accounts accordingly.
•
Reconciliation: Matching
bank
statements
to
financial
records
to
identify
discrepancies and ensure accuracy.
•
Financial reports: Generating basic financial statements like income statements
and balance sheets, providing a snapshot of the company’s financial health at a
specific time.
Bookkeepers are the meticulous record-keepers who ensure financial data is accurate, up-
to-date, and organized. Their work is essential for maintaining the integrity of a company’s
financial records and providing the raw data needed for accounting analysis.

Accountants take the raw data bookkeepers produce and transform it into meaningful
information. Their role involves:
•
Financial analysis: Examining a company’s financial data can reveal its financial
health, growth patterns, and competitive position. This involves calculating financial
ratios, tracking performance over time, and comparing results to industry
benchmarks.
•
Tax preparation: Calculating and filing tax returns accurately and on time, ensuring
compliance with tax laws and regulations.
•
Financial planning: Developing strategies to optimize financial resources and
improve overall performance. This includes creating and managing budgets, ensuring
efficient cash flow, and making sound investment decisions.
•
Compliance: Upholding accounting standards and regulations to ensure financial
integrity and transparency.
•
Auditing: Reviewing financial records to ensure accuracy and compliance, providing
assurance to stakeholders.

Some users of accounting information
•
Owners/ shareholders/ managers use the accounting information to assess the
financial position and performance and make informed decisions accordingly.
•
Investors use the accounting information to assess investment potential.
•
Lenders/ creditors/ banks use the accounting information to assess whether the
line of credit is sound.
•
Auditors use the accounting information to ensure internal controls are working
effectively and to prepare audit reports.
•
Tax authorities use the accounting information to assess tax liabilities.
•
Competitors use the accounting information to assess their own performance
against that of the business in the same Industry.

The essential requirements of accounting reports if they are to be useful for the
users are:
Clarity (understandability):
The reports are presented in such a way that reasonably-informed users can
comprehend their meaning, e.g. the use of headings and sub-headings may help to
highlight important information in a Profit and Loss Statement.
Accuracy (reliability):
The information should correspond with the actual underlying transactions and events,
and is capable of independent verification and is free from bias. The reports can be used
to confirm or correct expectations about past events and assist in forming, revising or
confirming expectations about the future.
Consistency (comparability):
Users must be able to identify similarities and differences between the current
information and information from previous years' reports or reports of different entities.
Timely
To be useful, the information prepared by accountants must also be timely i.e. reports
should be prepared in plenty of time for the people requiring the information to make
decisions. If information is not available when it is needed, it is of no use.
Compliance
Reports should comply with the requirements of accounting regulations and accounting
standards.

The Accounting Cycle
Overall, this Introduction to Accounting course will follow the accounting cycle through
each stage as a reference point with additional accounting concepts and fundamentals
added. Note also that this course refers to a manual accounting system as a
computerised accounting system automates some of the stages.
The accounting cycle refers to the regular repetition of a standardised set of stages
commencing once transactions occur and capturing the financial information in source
documents to the preparation of financial reports. It describes the sequence of events
once a transaction occurs. Refer to the accounting cycle flowchart 1 below for a visual
representation;

Flowchart 1

Accounting – Unit 0: Introduction and Accounting Cycle
Accounting | Page 4



The Accounting Cycle steps
The accounting cycle is a continual process because business activity is ongoing. The
source documents, journals, ledgers, financial reports and subsequent analysis are then
carefully stored in a safe place and/or archived as they may be required for future
reference, comparisons and/or taxation purposes.
Stage 1 - Transactions:
Transactions are events that alter the financial position of a business and require the
entering of information into accounting records. Generally, this involves activities of
buying, selling and/or exchanging of goods and services for cash or on credit.
Stage 2 - Source Documents
Source Documents are the original financial documents that contains evidence and/or
proof of transactions occurring. The transaction information and details are collected in
the form of source documents. Some commonly used source documents include;
invoices, cheques, receipts, credit notes, bank deposit slips and bank statements. These
source documents contain the details that will then be recorded in the journals.
Stage 3 - Journals
Journals are the first book of entry that are used to record details and information from
source documents.
Stage 4 - Ledgers
The ledger is a book of secondary entry and contains all the accounts of a business.
Information from the journals are posted (or transferred) to the corresponding accounts
in the ledger.
Ledgers include the General Ledger where values from the journals are entered and
Accounts Payable and Receivable Subsidiary Ledgers individually.
The accounts in the ledger can be presented in either T format or columnar format. The
accounts are also classified and grouped into five elements. These include the Assets,
Liabilities, Owner’s Equity, Revenue and Expenses of a business (refer to Lecture 3).
Stage 5 - Trial balance
The Trial Balance is a list of all the account balances in the General Ledger (after the
balancing process for each account is completed). Debit balances are listed in the debit
column of the Trial Balance and credit balances are listed in the credit column. The totals
for the debit and credit columns are calculated to check if they are equal. This ensures
that the accounting rules have been followed (ie double entry rule) and the equality of
the accounting equation has been maintained.
Stage 6 - Reports
The trial balance is used to prepare the financial reports of a business. The reports are
prepared at the end of the accounting period. The 2 main reports for the purposes of this
course are the Profit and Loss Statement and the Balance Sheet.

The Profit and Loss Statement is also known as the Income Statement or the
Statement of Financial Performance. It contains information about the revenues (R) and
expenses (E) of a business for a defined accounting period, hence the profit or loss (R-E)
of a business and how the business has performed.
The Balance Sheet or the Statement of Financial Position displays the assets, liabilities
and owner’s equity of the business at a point in time.
The Cash Flow Statement is a financial report that tracks the movement of cash into and
out of a business over a specific period, detailing how much cash is generated and spent
from operating, investing, and financing activities. Unlike an income statement that includes
non-cash transactions, a cash flow statement focuses solely on actual cash movements to
provide insight into a company's liquidity, financial health, and ability to meet its financial
obligations
After the financial statements are prepared and presented they are then analysed in
order to assess the profitability, liquidity, solvency and management effectiveness of the
business. The financial reports and their subsequent analysis will be used by interested
parties such as owners, managers, creditors and investors for informed decision making.
The accounting cycle then begins for the next accounting period.

Accounting Conventions
Development of Accounting
The double entry system was first outlined in the late 1400’s by Pacioli, a Franciscan
monk and mathematician. Accounting was used by merchants to record their
expenditure and to show 'what they had left’ (ie stewardship).

Over the centuries, the emphasis of accounting has changed from asking 'what
happened?' (collecting, recording and summarising) to 'what should we do?'
(analysing and reporting). The preparation of financial information for decision making
is now the key focus.

The nature of accounting has changed to meet the needs of different types and sizes
of businesses. Businesses can vary greatly in size - from sole traders to large
companies. They can be profit-making enterprises or not-for-profit organisations such
as clubs, charities or societies. Any organisation where money changes hands for
goods or services can be regarded as a business.

Businesses differ in their types of activities:

Service businesses provide a service, eg a motel, doctor, or education
providers.

Trading or merchandising businesses buy and sell goods, eg an
importer of shoes.

Manufacturing businesses purchase raw materials and produce products
to sell, eg shoe manufacturing.

Farming businesses use the land to produce food or raw materials eg
wool.

As the nature of commerce has changed, the demands on the accounting profession
have increased. Today the accounting system must cope with complicated and
changing tax laws and high-pressure business activity. It must assist in decision
making for all users of accounting information, from individuals and clubs to huge
multinational corporations and governments.

Accounting – Unit 2: Accounting Conventions
Accounting | Page 1



Sources of accounting regulation
Historically, the accounting system is based on a number of conventions and
doctrines. They provide a foundation for the accounting process. However, the
complexity of business activity found the conventions to be inadequate for the needs
of modern accounting. The need to provide more direction has given rise to the
development and implementation of Australian Accounting Standards and also
Statements of Accounting Concepts.

Conventions are practices or rules and accepted customs that have developed over
time in the accounting profession. They are practices concerned with preparing
and presenting financial information that is assumed by all accountants including
students. Some of these are listed below.

Monetary convention
Monetary measurement means that all information must be described in dollar terms.
Limitations:
Inflation makes comparisons difficult because the purchasing power of the dollar
changes from year to year. The changing value of the dollar means, for example, that
a profit of $10,000 in 1970 cannot be directly compared with a profit of $20,000 in
2020.

Some things cannot be measured in monetary terms, eg good management and
excellent employer-employee relations. These contribute greatly to the success of a
business but cannot be measured easily in dollar terms.

Accounting entity convention
There needs to be a clear boundary (from an accounting point of view) separating the
financial affairs of the accounting entity from other activities. For example, the
personal financial affairs of the owner of a business are kept separate from the affairs
of the business itself. All business transactions are recorded from the point of view of
the business, not the owner.

For example, John is the owner of the business Lighting Warehouse. The business has
cash $10,000, stock $16,000 and a bank loan $30,000. The assets of the business
total $56,000. John’s wedding ring worth $2,000 is not an asset of the business. It
is not included in the calculation of the business assets.

Continuity/Going concern convention
This convention assumes that a business is set up to continue indefinitely. Therefore
the assets other than stock for sale are assumed to be used in the operation rather
than sold for profit.

Historical cost convention
Assets are valued at the original purchase price and recorded at the actual amount.
Therefore, it is acceptable to use historical costs in the Statement of Financial
Position.

Accounting period convention
The life of a business is split into regular and equal intervals or periods, usually one
year or annually. This allows the business activities and performance to be measured.
Eg the accounting period could be from 1 July 2020 to 30 June 2021 (also known as
the financial year in Australia) or 1 January 2020 to 31 December 2020. The accounting
reports are prepared for the specific period to enable an assessment of the results from
trading, and a meaningful comparison with expected or past results.

Accounting – Unit 2: Accounting Conventions
Accounting | Page 2



Double Entry convention or Dual aspect convention
This convention states that each transaction has a minimum of two aspects and thus
a minimum of two accounts are affected. For example the introduction of cash as
capital will increase the asset (cash) and also increase the owner’s equity (capital).
Thus the purchase of a car for cash would result in an increase in the asset (car) and
a decrease in another asset (cash). Any of the five elements could be affected.
Applying the double entry convention helps to maintain the equality of the accounting
equation.

Consistency Convention
This is a principle that the same accounting principles should be used for
preparing financial statements over a number of time periods. This enables the
management to draw important conclusions regarding the working of the concern over
a longer period. It allows a comparison in the performance of different periods. If
different accounting procedures and processes are used for preparing financial
statements of different years then the results will not be comparable because these
will be based on different postulates.

Accrual Convention
An accounting system that tries to match the recognition of revenues earned with
the expenses incurred in generating those revenues. It ignores the timing of the cash
flows associated with revenues and expenses.

Cash Vs Accrual Accounting
1. Cash accounting – cash accounting is concerned with recording accounting
transactions at the time only when cash is received and cash is paid. As an
example this means recording revenue only when cash is received and
expenses when cash is paid. Most small businesses use this method.
2. Accrual accounting – accrual accounting is concerned with recording accounting
transactions at the time they take place irrespective of the exchange of cash. This
means that in an accounting period recording revenues as earned and expenses as
incurred regardless of cash being paid or received. This method uses the concept
of matching revenues and expenses in an accounting period as to when and how
to record transactions. Thus a sale of goods on credit gives rise to revenue and
accounts receivable and a purchase of goods on credit gives rise to purchases and
accounts payable in the accounting period. This method provides a more
meaningful profit/loss result and most medium/large businesses use this method.
 For most merchandising businesses, using the accrual basis of accounting means
recording revenues when goods are sold rather than when the cash is received.
For entities that generate revenue by providing services, the accrual basis of
accounting is typically applied by recording revenue when the service is performed
rather than when the customer or client pays for the service. If services are part
of a long-term contract, the revenue may need to be recognised progressively
over several periods. The accounting reports prepared using the accrual-based
system better reflect the true position and performance of the business for the
period covered by the accounting period.
The matching of Revenues and Expenses for the defined accounting period is an important
part of profit/loss measurement and the subsequent preparation of the Income Statement
and Balance Sheet. A business could use either of 2 accounting methods in order to record
transactions and determine their profit; cash accounting or accrual accounting.

Conservatism
Conservatism, or prudence, is a principle that dictates accountants should recognize potential
losses when they are possible, but only record potential gains when they are certain. This
practice ensures that financial statements are not misleading by overstating assets or income.

Accounting – Unit 2: Accounting Conventions
Accounting | Page 3



The revenue recognition principle
The revenue recognition principle is an accounting concept under accrual
accounting that states revenue should be recorded only when it has been earned and
is realized or realizable, regardless of when payment is received.

A basic accounting equation is used to implicitly express that Assets (A) equals Liabilities
(L) plus Owner’s Equity (OE). The accounting equation can thus be expressed as:
A = L + OE
Or
A – L = OE (this is also known as Net Assets)

•
Non-current assets are assets that will remain with the business for
longer than one accounting period. They will be used up over many
accounting periods.
Examples are equipment, furniture, motor vehicle, goodwill and investments.
Liabilities (L): what the business owes to persons or other businesses other than the
owners eg trade creditors and loans. Liabilities can be subdivided into current liabilities
and non-current liabilities.
•
Current liabilities are amounts owed to persons or businesses that have to
be repaid within one accounting year, for example, accounts payable
(creditors) and bank overdraft.
•
Non-current liabilities are commitments which do not need to be met
within twelve months of the balance date, for example, mortgage loans.

Revenues (R) are the income of the business. Revenue can be from different
sources such as sales, rent received, interest received, commission received,
discounts received, and service fees received. The accounts that keep record of such
revenue items are found in the general ledger of a business. They include sales,
rent received, interest received, commission received, discounts received and
service revenue.

Revenue items help to generate profit for the business and subsequently increases
owner’s equity.

Expenses (E) are outgoings or costs to pay for items that enable the business to
operate to continue earning income. Some examples of expenses are cost of goods
sold, wages, rent, bank fees, telephone and advertising.

Expenses decrease profits for the business and subsequently decreases owner’s equity
Owner’s Equity (OE): what the business owes its owners or what belongs to the owners
eg capital and drawings.
•
Capital is the amount the owner has put into or contributed to the business.
•
Drawings is a withdrawal of cash or stock from the business by the owner.
•
Any profit made by the business will increase the owner’s equity in the business.
•
Any loss incurred by the business will reduce the owner’s equity in the business.

Why do you have to separate into current or non current?

•
Clear presentation
•
To comply with accounting standards and regulations
•
Required for good business planning. For example the business should be aware
of the liquid assets in order to meet short debts or fund any future purchases
and/or investments.

Accounts associated with the income statement

An income statement (or a profit and loss statement) is another important financial
report of a business. It is a statement of the financial performance of a business over
a period of time. The income statement reports on the revenues (incomes) and
expenses of a business. Because the income statement reports on the revenues and
expenses, the accounts associated with these two groups are referred to as the
income statement accounts.

In general, the difference between the revenue (R) and expenses (E) is shown as
either a profit or a loss and usually the report is presented in the vertical format.

Revenues are the income of the business. Revenue can be from different sources
such as sales, rent received, interest received, commission received, discounts
received, and service fees received. The accounts that keep record of such revenue
items are found in the general ledger of a business. They include sales, rent
received, interest received, commission received, discounts received and service
revenue.
Revenue items help to generate profit for the business and subsequently increases
owner’s equity.

Expenses are outgoings or costs to pay for items that enable the business to operate
to continue earning income. Some examples of expenses are cost of goods sold,
wages, rent, bank fees, telephone and advertising.

Expenses decrease profits for the business and subsequently decreases owner’s equity.

Accounting


Accounts associated with the balance sheet

The balance sheet is an important financial report. It is a report or statement about
the financial position of a business as at a particular date. It is a detailed version of
the accounting equation. In report format, it is a listing of the assets owned by a
business, the liabilities of the business and the owner’s equity in the business.

•
Some examples of accounts in the asset element or group are cash at bank,
accounts receivable, stock, machinery, furniture, land and building, plant and
equipment and motor vehicles.
•
Some examples of accounts in the liability element or group are accounts
payable and loans.
•
Some examples of accounts in the owner’s equity element or group are capital
and drawings.

The Expanded Accounting Equation
The expanded equation can be represented as:
A + E = L + OE + R
or
A = L + OE + (R – E)
(R - E) represents the calculation of profit or loss.
If R > E, the business makes a profit. Profit is a reward for risk taking and is added to
the owner’s equity as it belongs to the owners.
If R < E, the business makes a loss. Losses reduce the owner’s equity as it also belongs
to the owners.
The (R – E) shows the relationship between the balance sheet and the income statement as
any profits or losses belong to the owners (owed to the owners).
A = L+OE is also presented by the balance sheet whilst (R-E) is presented by the income
statement and it has an effect on the balance sheet via OE.

Applying the double entry convention helps to maintain the equality of the accounting
equation. Equality of the accounting equation must be maintained at all times.

What is an account?

The basic recording unit. Each transaction is recorded into accounts. Accounts are the items
that are affected by the transaction. Accounts are the items that are affected by the
transaction and where transactions are subsequently recorded.

An account records any increase and decrease of assets, liabilities, revenue, expenses
and owner’s equity.

Accounts are found in the General Ledger. Accounts can be presented in either the T
format or the columnar format. As part of this course both formats will be discovered
and assessed. The overall and end results will be the same.

T-account
Accounts in T format are similar to the capital letter T with the name of an account
shown at the top. The left hand side of the T account is called the debit side and includes
column headings of the date, particulars and debit amount. The right hand side of the
T account is called the credit side and also includes column headings of the date,
particulars and credit amount. The particulars can also be called the description column
and is used to record the name of the corresponding account affected.

Double entry explained

Under the universally used double-entry system, the dual (two-sided) effect of each
transaction is recorded in appropriate accounts. This system provides a logical method for
recording transactions. The double-entry system also offers a means of ensuring the accuracy
of the recorded amounts. If every transaction is recorded with equal debits and credits, then
the sum of all the debits to the accounts must equal the sum of all the credits. The double-
entry system for determining the equality of the accounting equation is much more efficient
than the plus/minus procedure used earlier. Therefore, it was necessary after each transaction
to compare total assets with total liabilities and equity to determine the equality of the two
sides of the accounting equation.

Analyze transactions and prepare an analysis table

Recording transactions in the accounts requires following all the conventions and
concepts especially the double entry rule. The double entry rule requires that each
transaction affect at least two accounts; one on the debit side and the other on the
credit side. To decide which account has to be debited and which has to be credited,
each transaction has to be analysed. A table is drawn up to help analyse the transactions.
It is called an analysis chart.

revenue, expenses and owner’s equity.

Accounts payable is also known as creditors and is an example of current liabilities.
Accounts payable are businesses or persons from whom the business purchases trading

Accounts receivable is also known as debtors and is an example of current assets.

 E.g. Kingsford Trading sold toys to Princess Limited for $500, to be paid in 14

Note: The 2 methods of recording inventory transactions

1. Perpetual – this method involves the business keeping track of each inventory item
and purchases of inventory are recorded in the Inventory account. Once a sale of
goods occurs the original cost is transferred out of the inventory account and into
the expense account named Cost Of Goods Sold (COGS). This method allows the
business to calculate the Gross Profit (ie Sales – COGS) immediately. This method
usually suits businesses where the tracking of individual inventory items is feasible
and cost effective. This course will not use this method.

2. Periodic – this method involves the business recording the purchase of Inventory
into the expense account named Purchases. Therefore once a sale of goods occurs
no transaction is required to the Inventory account at that point in time. However,
at the end of the accounting period a stocktake is undertaken (a physical counting
of Inventory on hand/not sold) and this is used together with the Inventory at the
beginning of the accounting period to determine the Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)
and hence the Gross Profit. This method usually suits businesses where the
tracking of individual inventory items is not feasible and too costly. This course
will use this method only.

Journal Entries

Transactions are initially recorded in chronological order in a journal before they are transferred
to the accounts. For each transaction the journal shows the debit and credit effects on specific
accounts. Businesses may use various kinds of journals to record transactions; these are
explored in detail in chapter 6. Every business has at least the most basic form of journal, a
general journal. The general journal makes two significant contributions to the recording
process.

•
It provides a chronological record of all transactions.
•
It discloses in one place the complete effect of a transaction. This helps to prevent
or locate errors.

Entering transaction data in the journal is known as journalising.


Separate journal entries are made for each transaction. A complete entry consists of:
(1) the date of the transaction,
(2) the accounts and amounts to be debited and credited, and
(3) a brief explanation of the transaction, referred to as a narration.

Note the following features of the journal entries.

•
The date of the transaction is entered in the Date column.

•
The account to be debited is always entered first at the left.

•
The account to be credited is then entered on the next line, indented under the line above.
The indentation differentiates debits from credits and decreases the possibility of
switching the debit and credit amounts.

•
The amounts for the debits are recorded in the debit (left) column, and the amounts for
the credits are recorded in the credit (right) column.

•
A brief explanation of the transaction is given (narration). The narration is found directly
below the transaction.

It is important to use correct and specific account names and numbers in journal entries. Since
all accounts are used in preparation of the financial statements, erroneous account names lead

to incorrect financial statements. Some flexibility exists initially in selecting account names. For
example, a business could use any of these account names for recording the cost of delivery
trucks: delivery vehicles, delivery trucks or trucks. The main criterion is that each name must
appropriately describe the type of asset, liability, revenue, expense or equity represented in the
account.

Terms of payment



The credit terms specify the amount of the cash discount and time period during which it is
offered. They also indicate the time within which the purchaser is expected to pay the full invoice
price. In the sales invoice above, credit terms are 2.5% 7 days, n/30, meaning that a 2.5% cash
discount may be taken on the invoice price, less (‘net of’) any returns, if payment is made within
7 days of the invoice date (the discount period); otherwise, the invoice price, less any returns, is
due 30 days from the invoice date.

Discounts

Discount received: The credit terms of a purchase on account may permit the buyer to claim a
discount for prompt payment. The buyer calls this settlement discount - discount received. This
incentive offers advantages to both parties — the purchaser saves money, and the seller is able
to shorten the operating cycle by converting the accounts receivable into cash earlier.

The credit terms specify the amount of the cash discount and time period during which it is
offered. They also indicate the time within which the purchaser is expected to pay the full invoice
price.

When the seller elects not to offer a settlement discount for prompt payment, credit terms will
specify only the maximum time period for paying the balance due. For example, the time period
may be stated as n/30, meaning that the net amount must be paid in 30 days from the invoice
date.

When an invoice is paid within the discount period, the amount of the discount is credited to
discount received. Discounts are recorded by the buyer as revenue, as a discount represents a
saving in outflows and a consequential reduction in liabilities and an increase in equity.

Example: To illustrate, assume Sauk Stereo pays the balance due of $3500 (gross invoice price
of $3800 less purchase returns of $300) on 12 May, the last day of the discount period. The
settlement discount is $70 ($3500 × 2%), and the amount of cash paid by Sauk Stereo is $3430
($3500 − $70). The entry to record the 12 May payment by Sauk Stereo is shown below.

Trade discounts: Trade discounts, unlike settlement discounts, do not depend on early payment
of the amount due and are not recorded in the records of either the buyer or the seller. Trade
discounts are disclosed on the sales invoice as a percentage reduction in the list price of the
inventories sold.

For example, assume that a seller quotes a list price of $500 per item and allows a trade discount
of 10% for buyers who purchase in large quantities (in this example, assume that 8 items or more
are considered a large purchase). If the buyer purchases 10 items of inventory on 19 May, taking
a trade discount of 10%, the invoice price would be $4500 (10 × $500 × 90%). The purchase would
be recorded in the buyer’s records as:


Discount Allowed: The seller may offer the customer a settlement discount for the prompt
payment of the balance due. Like a purchase discount, a sales discount is based on the invoice
price less returns, if any. Businesses decide on the percentage of discount to be offered to
customers based on many factors, including rewarding valuable customers and encouraging
speedy payment. Businesses decide on the amount of discount to offer based on how much cash
they are willing to forgo while ensuring that the discount provides enough incentive for the
customer to pay within the discount period. The discount allowed account is increased (debited)
for discounts that are taken by customers.

The entry by PW Audio Supply Ltd to record the cash receipt on 12 May from Sauk Stereo within
the discount period is shown next.




Purchase

If Sauk Stereo pays the amount owing outside the discount period, PW Audio Supply Ltd
increases cash for $3500 and decreases accounts receivable for the same amount on the day
payment is received.


Discount allowed is reported as an expense in the statement of profit or loss and provides
information to management on the amount of discount taken by customers. Sellers offer
customers settlement discounts to encourage early payment of the account and have the cash
available for use by the business before the end of the credit period.

Bad debt Expense:
Although each customer must satisfy the credit requirements of the seller before the credit sale
is approved, inevitably some accounts receivable become uncollectable, i.e. the customer
defaults and never pays the account. For example, one of your customers may not be able to pay
because it experienced a decline in sales due to a downturn in the economy. Similarly, individuals
may be laid off from their jobs or be faced with unexpected hospital bills. Unrecoverable
receivables are known as bad debts expense. Such losses are considered a normal and
necessary risk of doing business on a credit basis.

Assume, for example, that Warden Pty Ltd writes off M.E. Doran’s $200 balance as uncollectable
on 12 December.

Adjusting Entries

In order for revenues and expenses to be recorded in the correct accounting period, adjusting
entries are made to revenue and expense accounts at the end of the accounting period. In short,
adjusting entries are needed to ensure that the recognition criteria are followed for assets,
liabilities, revenues and expenses.

The use of adjusting entries makes it possible to produce accurate financial statements at the
end of the accounting period. Thus, the statement of financial position reports appropriate
assets, liabilities and equity at the end of the reporting period, and the statement of profit or loss
shows the appropriate profit (or loss) for the period. Adjusting entries are necessary because
the general ledger may not contain up-to-date and complete data, for the following reasons.

Some events are not journalised daily because it would not be useful or efficient to do so.
Examples are depreciation and the earning of wages by employees.

Some costs are not journalised during the accounting period because the economic benefits
expire with the passage of time rather than as a result of recurring daily transactions. Examples
include building and equipment deterioration, rent and insurance.

Some items may be unrecorded. An example is an electricity or telephone bill that will not be
received until the next accounting period.

Adjusting entries are required every time financial statements are prepared. An essential
starting point is an analysis of each account in the trial balance to determine whether it is
complete and up to date for financial statement purposes.

Adjusting entries can be classified as either prepayments or accruals. Each of these classes
has two subcategories as shown below:

Prepayments
Prepaid expenses: Amounts paid in cash and recorded as assets until the economic benefits
are used or consumed.

Unearned Revenue/Revenue received in advance: Amounts received from customers and
recorded as liabilities until the services are performed or the goods are provided and revenue is
recognised.

Accruals
Accrued revenues: Amounts not yet received and not yet recorded for which the goods or

Accounting

services have been provided.

Accrued expenses: Amounts not yet paid and not yet recorded for which the consumption of
economic benefits has occurred.

Prepaid Expenses
Payments of amounts that will provide economic benefits for more than the current accounting
period are called prepaid expenses or prepayments. When such a cost is incurred, an asset
account is increased (debited) to show the service or benefit that will be received in the future.
Examples of common prepayments are insurance, supplies, advertising and rent.

Prepaid expenses expire as the service is provided with the passage of time (e.g. rent and
insurance) or through use (e.g. supplies). The expiration of these benefits does not require daily
entries — that would be impractical and unnecessary. Accordingly, we postpone the recognition
of the expiry of prepaid expenses until financial statements are prepared. At the end of each
reporting period, adjusting entries are made to record the expenses applicable to the current
accounting period and to show the remaining amounts in the asset accounts. Before
adjustment, assets are overstated and expenses are understated. Therefore, an adjusting entry
for prepaid expenses results in an increase (a debit) to an expense account and a decrease (a
credit) to an asset account.

Prepaid Expense: Example: Insurance
Entities purchase insurance to protect themselves from losses due to fire, theft and other
unforeseen events. Insurance must be paid in advance, usually for a period of 1 year. Insurance
payments (premiums) made in advance are normally recorded in the asset account prepaid
insurance. At the end of the reporting period it is necessary to increase (debit) insurance
expense and decrease (credit) prepaid insurance for the cost of insurance that has expired
during the period.

On 4 October Wong Pty Ltd paid $600 for a 1-year insurance policy. Coverage began on 1
October. The payment was recorded by increasing (debiting) prepaid insurance when it was
paid. This account shows a balance of $600 in the 31 October trial balance. An analysis of the
policy reveals that $50 ($600/12) of insurance expires each month. The expiration of prepaid
insurance has the following effect on the accounting equation in October (and each of the next
11 months):




Unearned Revenue/Revenue Received in Advance
Cash received before the revenue recognition criteria have been met is recorded by increasing
(crediting) a liability account called revenues received in advance. Items such as rent and
customer deposits for future service result in unearned revenue. Airlines such as Qantas and
Virgin Australia treat receipts from the sale of tickets as unearned revenue until the flight service
is provided. Health clubs treat membership revenue as deferred income until the service has
been provided in accordance with the membership contract. Unearned revenue is the opposite
of prepaid expenses.

When payment is received for services to be provided in a future accounting period, an unearned
revenue (a liability) account should be credited to recognise the obligation that exists. Unearned
revenues are subsequently recognised as revenue when the service is provided to a customer.

Accounting

During the accounting period, it is not always practical to make daily entries to the unearned
revenue accounts as the services are provided. Instead, we delay recognition of revenue until
the adjustment process. Then an adjusting entry is made to record the revenue during the period
and to show the liability that remains at the end of the accounting period.

Wong Pty Ltd received $1200 on 2 October from R. Knox for advertising services expected to be
completed by 31 December. The payment was credited to service revenue received in advance,
and this liability account shows a balance of $1200 in the 31 October trial balance. An evaluation
of the work performed by Wong for Knox indicated that services worth $400 were performed in
October.



Depreciation
A business typically owns a variety of assets that have long lives, such as buildings, equipment
and motor vehicles. These assets are called non-current assets as they provide future economic
benefits to the business for more than one accounting period. The term useful life of the asset
refers to the estimated total service potential or estimated period of time over which the future
economic benefits are expected to be consumed by the entity. Because a building is expected
to provide service for many years, it is recorded as an asset, rather than an expense, on the date
it is acquired. As explained in chapter 1, such assets are recorded at cost, as required by the
historical cost principle. According to expense recognition criteria, a portion of this cost should
then be reported as an expense during each period of the asset’s useful life. Depreciation is the
process of allocating the cost of an asset to expense over its useful life.

Need for adjustment:  From an accounting standpoint, the acquisition of long-lived assets is
essentially a long-term prepayment for economic benefits. The need for making periodic
adjusting entries for depreciation is therefore the same as described before for other prepaid
expenses — that is, to recognise the cost of economic benefits that have been consumed during
the period as expenses and to report the cost of economic benefits that remain at the end of the
period as assets. One point is very important to understand: depreciation is an allocation
concept, not a valuation concept. That is, we depreciate an asset to allocate its cost to the
periods in which we use the asset. We are not attempting to reflect the actual change in the
value of the asset.

For Wong Pty Ltd, assume that depreciation on the office equipment is estimated to be $480 a
year, or $40 per month. This would have the following impact on the accounting equation:


The balance in the accumulated depreciation account will increase by $40 each month.

Statement presentation: Accumulated depreciation—office equipment is a contra asset
account, which means that it is offset against office equipment on the statement of financial
position, and its normal balance is a credit. This account is used instead of decreasing
(crediting) office equipment in order to record both the original cost of the equipment and the
total cost that has expired to date. In the statement of financial position, accumulated
depreciation—office equipment is deducted from the related asset account as shown below:

Accounting




The difference between the cost of any depreciable asset and its related accumulated
depreciation is referred to as its carrying amount (also referred to as book value). The carrying
amount of the equipment at the end of the reporting period is $4960.

Accrued Revenue
Accrued revenues are revenues that are recorded as adjusting entries because they have not
been recorded in the daily recording of transactions. Accrued revenues may accumulate
(accrue) over time, as in the case of rent revenue and interest revenue, or they may result from
services that have been performed but neither invoiced nor collected, as in the case of
commissions and fees. The former are unrecorded because the receipt of rent and interest
revenues does not involve daily transactions. Fee revenue, or service revenue, may be
unrecorded because only a portion of the total service has been provided and the clients won’t
be invoiced until the service has been completed. Alternatively, commissions revenue may be
due but not received by the end of the reporting period.

An adjusting entry is required to show the receivable that exists at the end of the reporting period
and to record the revenue for the period. Before adjustment, both assets and revenues are
understated. Accordingly, an adjusting entry for accrued revenues results in an increase (a debit)
to an asset account and an increase (a credit) to a revenue account.

Wong Pty Ltd earns commission of 1% of sales revenue from one of its advertising clients.
Although the client has not yet paid, Wong has been advised that the amount for October is
$200. As this revenue has not yet been recorded, revenue and assets are understated.




Accrued Expense
Expenses not yet paid or recorded at the end of the reporting period are called accrued
expenses. Interest, rent, taxes and salaries are common examples of accrued expenses.
Accrued expenses result from the same factors as accrued revenues. In fact, an accrued
expense in the records of one business is likely to be an accrued revenue to another business.
For example, the $200 accrual of service revenue by Wong Pty Ltd is an accrued expense to the
client that received the service.

Adjustments for accrued expenses are necessary to record the obligations that exist at the end
of the reporting period and to recognise the expenses that apply to the current accounting
period. Before adjustment, both liabilities and expenses are understated. Therefore, an adjusting
entry for accrued expenses results in an increase (a debit) to an expense account and an
increase (a credit) to a liability account.

Accrued Expenses: Example 1: Accrued Salaries
Some types of expenses, such as employee salaries and commissions, are paid for after the

services have been performed. At Wong Pty Ltd, salaries were last paid on 26 October; the next
payment of salaries will not occur until 9 November. As shown in the calendar, 3 working days
remain in October (29–31 October). (Accrued salaries can also be termed accrued wages.)





Wong Pty Ltd pays salaries every 2 weeks. Consequently, the next payday is 9 November, when
total salaries of $4000 will again be paid. The payment consists of $1200 of salaries payable at

On 1 October Wong Pty Ltd borrowed $5000 from a bank, with interest payments required
quarterly. The bank charges Wong Pty Ltd interest at an annual rate of 12%. The amount of the

The general journal provides a chronological list of all of the transactions for a business. A
chronological list on its own, however, is of limited use. Classifying and summarising data
improves their usefulness for decision making. For example, a business’s general journal could
contain hundreds of purchases, cash receipts and cash payments transactions in any given month.
If a sales manager wants to know the total sales revenue for any particular month, this information
cannot be easily obtained from the general journal, but it can be obtained from the sales revenue
account in the ledger. The ledger accumulates all the information about changes in specific
account balances such as sales revenue, cash, and wages expense.

The entire group of accounts maintained by a business is referred to collectively as the general
ledger. A general ledger contains all the assets, liabilities and equity accounts, as shown below.

Accounting – Unit 5: Ledger Accounts – T-format

T-format vs Column format

Accounts are found in the General Ledger. Accounts can be presented in the T format or the
columnar format. Once a transaction is analysed, entries can be made to the related accounts and
the double entry rule followed.
Accounts in T format are similar to the capital letter T with the name of an account shown at the top of
the T. The left hand side of the T account is called the debit side and includes column headings of the
date, particulars and debit amount. The right hand side of the T account is called the credit side and
also includes column headings of the date, particulars and credit amount. The particulars can also be
called the description column and is used to record the name of the corresponding account affected.

The main differences between the T and columnar formats are the one date and particular columns, the debit

Balancing in T-format

(Note: b/d = brought down, c/d = carried down)

Once recording is complete, a trial balance is prepared. To facilitate this process, the balance of each account
in the general ledger must be calculated. The process of balancing a T account is illustrated using the cash
account below. Balancing involves the following main steps:
•
For each account, add each side. Generally, the normal account balance side will be larger - (Debit side
for Assets, Expenses & Drawings, Credit side for Liabilities, Owner’s Equity & Revenue)
•
The closing balance for the account can now be determined by subtracting the amounts listed on the
lesser side from the total. The words ‘balance c/d or closing balance’ and the amount calculated in this
step are recorded on the lesser side (generally the side opposite to the normal balance side).
•
The date (the first day of the next month), the words ‘balance b/d or opening balance’ and the balance
calculated in step 3 are written below the ruled-off lines on the greater account balance side (usually the
normal balance side).

Balancing a T format account -Illustration
The balance of an account is essentially the difference between the debit side and the credit side of
the account. If the debit side adds up to be greater than the credit side, the balance is called a debit
balance. If, on the other hand, the credit side adds up to be greater than the debit side, the difference
is a credit balance. The T format account requires periodic balancing. This is a disadvantage.

To balance an account, the following steps should be followed. A Cash at Bank Account is used
as an example to illustrate how to balance an account.

Find the total of the debit side. The debit total is $16,000 (15,000 + 1,000 = 16,000).
Find the total of the credit side. The credit total is $3,120 (500 + 2,000 + 60
+ 560 = 3,120).
Find the difference by subtracting the smaller total from the bigger total. The difference is
$12,880 (16,000 – 3,120 = 12,880).
Place the difference under the side that has a smaller total. In this example,
$12,880 is placed under the credit side. This difference is noted as Balance to be
carried down or simply Balance c/d for short.
Then total up the debit side, write down the total ($16,000) with a double underline.
Then total up the credit side, write down the total ($16,000) with a double underline.
•
At the start of the next period, the balance is brought down to the opposite side and is
noted as Balance b/d for short.
